findings.title: Delete uses d.Log instead of log with structured fields
findings.body: In `Delete`, `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` is used, while Create/Update/DeleteCollection/DeleteCollection all use `klog.NewContext(ctx, log)` where `log` includes `name`, `kind`, and `method` fields. The metric label is supposed to be the Kind, so this passes a different value into the same label, producing inconsistent time series in the dual_writer_* metrics.

findings.title: Async legacy writes inherit cancelled request context
findings.body: Each async legacy call derives its context from the incoming `ctx` via `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`. When the API caller cancels or times out, the parent `ctx` is already cancelled, so the child context is cancelled immediately and the legacy write never happens. The PR description frames legacy writes as a "safe measure" to keep legacy store in sync, but under request cancellation (which is common for slow upstream) the legacy side will drift from unified storage silently. The async legacy write should be derived from a non-cancelled context (e.g. `context.Background()` with timeout) so it survives caller disconnection.

findings.title: Async legacy failures are not logged
findings.body: Inside the goroutines that perform the asynchronous legacy Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection, the only signal on failure is the metrics counter (`recordLegacyDuration(... true ...)`); there is no `log.Error(...)` call. If unified storage diverges from legacy (the very thing mode 3 is supposed to mitigate), operators will see no log line and no test will detect the failure because errors are swallowed. Add `log.Error(err, "async legacy ... failed")` (or equivalent) inside each goroutine after the legacy call.

findings.title: Mode3 tests do not verify the asynchronous legacy writes
findings.body: Mode 3's defining behaviour is that writes go to storage synchronously and then to legacy asynchronously. None of `TestMode3_Create`, `TestMode3_Update`, `TestMode3_Delete`, or `TestMode3_DeleteCollection` actually asserts the legacy mock was called. `setupLegacyFn` sets up `m.On(...)` expectations but there is no `m.AssertExpectations(t)` (and the async goroutine may run after the test function returns). The Create and Update tests register legacy expectations that may simply never be exercised, and the Delete/DeleteCollection tests don't even register them. Without synchronization (e.g. wait group, channel, or retry on the mock) plus `AssertExpectations`, a regression that removes the async legacy call entirely would still pass the test suite.

findings.title: Mode3 read tests do not verify legacy is bypassed

The Mode1 Get test does check this for storage (`us.AssertNotCalled(...)`); the analogous assertion for mode 3 (legacy must not be called) is missing. A bug that silently falls back to legacy on reads would not be caught.

findings.title: TestMode3_Get creates a local prometheus registry
findings.body: `TestMode3_Get` calls `p := prometheus.NewRegistry()` locally even though a package-level `p` already exists (used by every other test in the file, and now exclusively by `TestMode1_Get` after this PR). The local registry is unused by the assertions in the test and just creates inconsistency. Use the package-level `p` like the rest of the suite.

findings.title: Destroy does not wait for in-flight async legacy writes
findings.body: `Destroy` calls `d.Storage.Destroy()` and `d.Legacy.Destroy()` immediately, but there is no synchronization with the goroutines launched by Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection. If a shutdown happens while async legacy writes are still pending (within their 10 s timeout), they will run against destroyed backends, producing confusing errors or panics. Consider tracking the goroutines with a `sync.WaitGroup` (or similar) and waiting for them in `Destroy` (with a bounded timeout).
